## Overview

The Bororo, who call themselves *Boe*, are an Indigenous people of Brazil living mainly in the state of Mato Grosso. They also extended into Bolivia and the Brazilian state of Goiás. Western Bororo communities lived around the Jauru and Cabaçal rivers, while Eastern Bororo communities, also called *Orarimogodoge*, lived in the region of the São Lourenço, Garças, and Vermelho Rivers. The Bororo live in eight villages, and their population is estimated at just under two thousand. They speak Bororo, a language in the Bororo language family of the Macro-Ge language family, and are mainly animistic in belief. Their social organization, circular village arrangement, life-cycle ceremonies, funerary rites, mythology, and language have received particular attention from anthropologists, including Claude Lévi-Strauss.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

They state only that men may have obligations to make ornamental items for their bride’s brother after marriage.

### Architecture

Bororo homes are traditionally arranged in a circle, forming a central courtyard that functions as an important social and religious space. The village, or *aldeia*, is divided into the exogamic halves *Exerae* and *Tugarége*, each of which is divided into four clans. The sources describe homes as having interior divisions between family spaces, with more private areas at the ends and a shared central space used for visits, small daily rituals, and meals. Doors and windows are usually left open, except during certain rituals and mourning. During mourning, the house is emptied and destroyed at the end of the funerals.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources mention the piercing of the ears and lips as one of the Bororo’s rituals. They also state that men may be required to make ornamental items for their bride’s brother after marriage.

## Music & performance

They do document a ceremonial dance filmed in 1930 by a party searching for the missing explorer Percy Fawcett. A surviving 32-minute silent film records the dance, a first-contact scenario with Boboré villagers, and Bororo men experiencing sympathetic labor pains.

## Dance & theatre

A ceremonial dance is documented in a 32-minute silent film made during a 1930 expedition searching for Percy Fawcett. The film also records a first-contact scenario with Boboré villagers and Bororo men experiencing sympathetic labor pains.

## Festivals & rituals

The Bororo practice several rituals and rites of passage. The Corn Festival celebrates the gathering of cereal, described as an important food in Indigenous foodways. Other listed rituals include the piercing of the ears and lips and a funeral ritual regarded as a sacred celebration by those who consider themselves Indigenous. The principal rites of passage are the naming ceremony, initiation, and funerary rites.

Funerary rites can last up to two months and have attracted ethnological attention because of their complexity. During mourning, women cannot attend certain rituals held inside the house. The house is emptied throughout the mourning period and destroyed at the end of the funerals.

## Foodways

The sources describe a historical shift from hunting and gathering toward agriculture. Under the influence of missionaries and, more recently, Brazilian authorities, agriculture became the basis of subsistence. Men hunt, while women—especially in the Rio Vermelho region—plant and harvest cassava, maize, and rice. Because agriculture is practiced by women, their importance has increased, particularly as game has become scarce.

The Corn Festival is associated with cereal gathering, and maize is identified as an important food.

## Oral tradition & literature

Bororo mythology features extensively in Claude Lévi-Strauss’s book *The Raw and the Cooked*. The sources also describe a totemic conception in which the Bororo are presented as identifying with red macaws, or *araras*. The quoted discussion states that this is understood as an essential identity rather than merely a name or proclaimed relationship.

## Language & religion

The Bororo speak Bororo Proper, which belongs to the Bororo language family within the Macro-Ge language family. The Bororo call their original language *Boe Wadáru*. The language is written in the Latin script, and literacy rates are under 30 percent. Most of the population today speaks Portuguese and Bororo. The language is spoken in Brazil, principally in Mato Grosso and in the villages of Meruri, Sangradouro, and Perigera. The sources state that Bororo language use was forbidden in the towns of Merai and Sangradouro toward the end of the 1960s while the Salesian mission operated there, after which it was restored and bilingual education was introduced.

The Bororo are mainly animistic in belief. They associate body odor with a person’s life force and breath odor with the person’s soul. The sources also describe Christianization by Salesian missionaries as a historical process that contributed to the reduction of Bororo linguistic and cultural heritage.
